strengths: The proposed RS-CL is a simple, lightweight, and clearly motivated auxiliary objective that directly targets the identified misalignment between VLM representations and robotic (proprioceptive) signals; the design (soft weights from state distances in Eq. 3-4, summarization token, representation-level view cutoff) is well-justified and easy to integrate into existing VLA pipelines.

Empirical validation is unusually comprehensive for this class of method: fine-tuning experiments on RoboCasa-Kitchen (3 dataset scales, 24 tasks, 1200 evaluation trials) and LIBERO, real-robot experiments on a Franka arm with in-domain, visual/physical generalization, and language-grounding evaluations, and from-scratch experiments across multiple VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T N1.5 VLM).

Gains are consistent across settings (+4.8 to +11.2 points on RoboCasa-Kitchen averages, +13.3 points on real robots), with the largest gains precisely on pick-and-place/precision tasks, which supports the paper's causal claim that proprioceptive alignment improves positioning accuracy.

The paper rules out simple explanations for the improvement: Table 3a shows vanilla InfoNCE (no soft labels) yields smaller gains, and Table 3b shows view cutoff beats token/feature/span cutoffs; Table 5/6 (CL vs. RS-CL) and the CKNNA analysis (Fig. 8) provide mechanistic evidence that representations actually align to robot states.

Reproducibility is well treated: hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, dataset links, training/inference details, layer-selection ablations, and real-robot hardware/evaluation protocols are all provided; limitations (e.g., not using object pose or contact forces) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest: the method is essentially a soft-weighted supervised InfoNCE (Khosla et al., 2020; Suresh & Ong, 2021) combined with a cutoff-style augmentation (Shen et al., 2020) applied at the representation level; the contribution is more a careful adaptation/combination than a new learning principle.

No variance/statistical significance reporting: simulation results (Tables 1-3, 5-10) appear to come from single runs with no seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars; some per-task comparisons (e.g., several LIBERO suites, some RoboCasa tasks in Table 7) are within noise of the baseline, which weakens the reliability of the smaller average gains.

Gains on LIBERO are comparatively small (+0.7 points average) and the authors attribute the weaker CL effect there to a smaller contrastive batch size, but this hyperparameter sensitivity of contrastive objectives is not systematically studied.

There is an inconsistency in the reported pick-and-place numbers: the introduction states 30.3% to 41.5% (+11.2%) while the abstract and Table 1 report 30.8% to 41.5%; the framing of deltas also conflates percentage points with percentages in places.

The fine-tuning experiments only test the frozen-VLM + adapter setting (following GEAR); it is unclear whether RS-CL remains beneficial when the VLM backbone is fully fine-tuned end-to-end, which is the more common VLA training regime in the cited literature (π0, π0-FAST).
The cosine decay of λ to 0 is an important design choice (RS-CL is effectively turned off late in training) but no ablation of the schedule or λ sensitivity is provided.
Real-robot evaluations use 24 trials per task, which is small for individual task comparisons despite the aggregate trends being convincing.
No explicit code release is promised, which limits immediate reproducibility of the from-scratch experiments even though implementation details are thorough.

strengths: The method is simple, lightweight, and well-motivated: using distances between proprioceptive states as soft supervision in a supervised InfoNCE objective is a clean way to inject control-relevant structure into VLA conditioning representations.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this type of contribution: fine-tuning on two established benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen, LIBERO) at three demonstration scales, real-robot experiments on a Franka arm (in-domain, visual/physical generalization, language grounding), from-scratch experiments across six-plus pre-trained backbones, and ablations over supervision targets, augmentation strategies, hidden layers, and batch size effects.

The gain on the hardest, positioning-sensitive tasks is meaningful (e.g., +11.2% on RoboCasa pick-and-place at 30 demos; +13.3% on real-robot tasks), and the paper is transparent that contrastive regularization alone (CL, Table 5/6) contributes part of the improvement while the state-based soft weighting adds the rest.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: hyperparameters, training schedules, datasets, checkpoints, evaluation protocols (1200 trials per RoboCasa condition, 50 trials per LIBERO task), and an explicit algorithm block are provided, along with an honest limitations and LLM-usage statement.

The analysis that alternative soft targets (next action distances) underperform current-state distances, and that this is plausibly because next actions are already the prediction target, is a genuinely useful empirical insight for future auxiliary-objective design.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The core technique is a soft-label-weighted supervised contrastive loss (Khosla et al., 2020; Suresh & Ong, 2021) combined with a cutoff-style augmentation (Shen et al., 2020); the contribution is primarily an application of known tools to VLA training rather than a new understanding or mechanism. The related work itself shows substantial overlap with R3M, VIP, CoRL-style contrastive robotics objectives.

A critical baseline is missing: a simple auxiliary regression loss predicting the proprioceptive state (or the next action) from the summarization embedding. Given that RS-CL's supervision signal is exactly this state, a plain predictive auxiliary loss is the obvious minimal competitor, and its absence leaves open whether the contrastive formulation is actually necessary or whether any state-grounding signal would suffice.

No seed/variance reporting anywhere. RoboCasa results are averages over 1200 trials, but all conditions appear to be single training runs; several headline gaps (e.g., +0.7% on LIBERO average, +4.0% at 300 demos) could plausibly fall within run-to-run variance. Real-robot results use only 24 trials per task, which is thin for claims of +13.3%.

The framing overstates the mechanism: in the main fine-tuning setup the VLM is frozen and only a lightweight adapter and projector are trained, so the method regularizes adapter features rather than 'VLM representations' as repeatedly claimed. The paper would be more precise about what representation is being shaped.

Effects are inconsistent across settings: on LIBERO the plain contrastive baseline (CL) actually slightly hurts (95.3 vs 95.7), gains are small relative to RoboCasa, and the paper attributes this post hoc to batch size. This weakens the claimed robustness of the approach and suggests sensitivity to training configuration (batch 32 vs 64 is chosen per benchmark, raising tuning concerns).

Minor consistency and presentation issues: the pick-and-place improvement is quoted as 30.8%→41.5% in the abstract but 30.3%→41.5% in Section 3.1 (Table 1 shows 30.8); several grammatical errors ('shown its capabilities', 'an promising'); and no code release is stated despite the reproducibility statement.

strengths: The method (RS-CL) is simple, lightweight, and well-motivated: the paper provides a clear diagnosis of the problem (VLM embeddings dominated by visual appearance rather than robot state, illustrated in Fig. 2) and a principled remedy via a soft-supervised InfoNCE variant weighted by proprioceptive state distances (Eq. 3-4).

Evaluation breadth is a decisive strength: consistent gains on two standard simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa-Kitchen across 30/100/300 demos; LIBERO), real-robot experiments with generalization tests, and from-scratch experiments across many VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T N1.5, RoboBrain, VeBrain, Cosmos-Reason1, NORA), which supports the claim that the approach generalizes beyond a single model.

Useful ablations: soft-label target choice (Table 3a), augmentation strategy (Table 3b), CL vs. RS-CL decomposition (Tables 5-6), layer ablations (Table 4), and a CKNNA analysis (Fig. 8) that provides mechanistic evidence that the representation space actually aligns with proprioceptive states.

The approach is practically attractive: it operates at the representation level with a summarization token and view cutoff, requiring no additional VLM forward passes, extra training stages, or curated datasets, and it composes with existing VLA pipelines and further-trained embodied VLM baselines.

Reproducibility is handled reasonably well: hyperparameters, training schedules, dataset links, and real-robot task definitions are documented in appendices, along with an algorithm box and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is insufficient for the headline claims. Simulation results appear to be single runs with no seeds or variance estimates; notably, the LIBERO improvement (95.7% to 96.4%) and several RoboCasa averages (+3-5%) could fall within run-to-run variance for VLA fine-tuning. The abstract's emphasized pick-and-place gain (30.8% to 41.5%) is more convincing, but no confidence intervals or repeated-seed results are given anywhere.

Real-robot evaluation uses only 24 trials per task, which limits the precision of per-task claims (e.g., 50.0% vs. 54.2% differences are essentially noise at this trial count); the aggregate +13.3% figure pools tasks with very different baselines (e.g., Plate to Basket jumps from 41.7% to 66.6%).

Novelty is moderate: the core idea is a soft-weighted supervised contrastive loss (combining InfoNCE with distance-based soft labels, following Khosla et al. 2020 and Suresh & Ong 2021) applied to VLA conditioning representations; the summarization token and view cutoff are sensible but incremental engineering. The contribution is more a well-executed application than a fundamentally new technique.

TheLIBERO results weaken the narrative somewhat: plain CL (InfoNCE + view cutoff) actually performs slightly below baseline (95.3% vs. 95.7%, Table 6), and the authors attribute the small RS-CL gain to batch size; this suggests sensitivity to training configuration that is not fully characterized (no ablation on λ schedule, batch size dependence beyond a remark in Appendix D.1, or sensitivity to τ and β beyond fixed values).

Fine-tuning experiments are confined to a single base VLA (GR00T N1.5); it would strengthen the paper to show RS-CL also improves π0-style models, since the fine-tuning story is central to the claimed practical impact.

Some design choices are under-justified: why Euclidean distance on mixed proprioceptive quantities (position, 6D rotation, gripper) is appropriate as a similarity signal, and why the weighting decays λ to zero (making the method partially a warm-up regularizer) is not analyzed; the potential that gains come mainly from early-training regularization rather than lasting representation change could be examined further.

strengths: Strong and comprehensive empirical validation: RS-CL is evaluated in fine-tuning (GR00T N1.5 on RoboCasa-Kitchen and LIBERO), from-scratch training across multiple pre-trained VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T), an autoregressive VLA variant (pi0-FAST, Table 10), and real-robot experiments on a Franka arm, showing consistent gains (e.g., 65.7 -> 69.7 on RoboCasa, 45.0 -> 58.3 real-robot average).

The central hypothesis (VLM representations are dominated by visual appearance rather than control-relevant signals) is supported by dedicated analysis: t-SNE visualizations (Fig. 2, 14), KNN task-phase classification (Table 5: 1.2% -> 22.9% vs. 25.6% proprioceptive upper bound), and CKNNA alignment measurements (Fig. 8). This goes beyond simply reporting downstream success rates.

Efficiency of the method is well characterized: the view-cutoff augmentation operates at the representation level with negligible overhead (+1.25% wall-clock, Table 6), and the paper fairly compares against TCN baselines showing they cost ~3x FLOPs for smaller gains (Table 3).

Thorough ablations: soft-label target definitions (Table 4a), augmentation strategies (Table 4b), hyperparameter sensitivity including multiple seeds (Table 8), hidden-layer selection (Table 7), state parameterizations and higher-dimensional embodiments (Table 11), and task-group breakdown (Table 12).

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed training recipes, hyperparameters, publicly available checkpoints/datasets, and evaluation protocol (1200 trials for RoboCasa, 50 per LIBERO task, 24 per real task).
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix E.6) acknowledging that only proprioceptive signals are used and that open/close tasks see smaller gains, plus an appropriate impact statement.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is a weighted supervised contrastive loss (soft labels from state distances, Khosla et al. 2020 / Suresh & Ong 2021) combined with a cutoff-style augmentation (Shen et al. 2020) applied at the feature level. The contribution is primarily a careful adaptation and empirical demonstration rather than a new technique.

Potential information leakage / redundancy concern is underexplored: the proprioceptive state q is already provided as input to the action decoder, so aligning VLM embeddings to q could partially duplicate information the decoder already receives. The paper does not clearly disentangle whether gains come from better representation structure vs. a regularization/annealing effect of the auxiliary loss (the cosine decay of lambda from 1 to 0 hints at the latter, but this is not analyzed).

Ablation gaps: Table 4a shows vanilla InfoNCE gives 67.7 vs. 69.7 for current-state soft labels, and feature cutoff gives 67.5 vs. 69.7 for view cutoff; these deltas (~2-3%) are meaningful but modest relative to run-to-run variability (seeds span 51.3-54.7 in Table 8), and the paper does not report confidence intervals for the headline RoboCasa comparisons.

Real-robot evaluation is limited in scale: 24 trials per task, some in-domain comparisons have overlapping error bars (e.g., Box to Plate 50.0 vs 54.2, Close Lid partial 29.2 vs 37.5), and the task suite is confined to tabletop pick-and-place/close-lid on one robot.

Some claims are broader than the evidence: the assertion that 'robotics-specific training alone may not fully close the gap' (Fig. 7) rests on a handful of adapted backbones of varying quality, and the mechanism behind why current-state distance outperforms next-action-sequence (DTW) supervision is speculative ('multimodal characteristics').

The paper does not discuss potential negative effects of pulling representations toward proprioceptive similarity on tasks where visual context (not robot state) determines the correct action, beyond noting preserved scene-classification accuracy.

strengths: The proposed RS-CL is lightweight and well-motivated: it operates at the representation level (learnable summarization token + projection head) and adds negligible compute overhead (+1.25% wall-clock, Table 6), making it genuinely easy to plug into existing VLA pipelines.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: fine-tuning on RoboCasa-Kitchen across 30/100/300 demonstrations (Fig. 4, Table 13), LIBERO (Table 2), real-robot experiments with in-domain and generalization splits (Fig. 6), from-scratch training across eight VLM backbones including robotics-adapted ones (Fig. 7), and adaptation to a second action model (π₀-FAST, Table 10).

The paper goes beyond headline success rates with mechanistic analyses: representation visualizations (Fig. 2/14), KNN task-phase classification (Table 5, Table 9), and CKNNA alignment curves (Fig. 8) collectively support the central hypothesis that VLM embeddings are organized by visual scene rather than control-relevant state.

Thorough ablations separate the contributions: soft-label target definitions (Table 4a), augmentation strategies (Table 4b), comparison against TCN baselines with FLOPs accounting (Table 3), and a detailed hyperparameter/seed sensitivity study (Table 8).
Limitations and future directions are discussed honestly (App. E.6), and implementation/hyperparameter details are documented at a level that supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest. The method is essentially a weighted supervised InfoNCE (soft-label contrastive learning of Suresh & Ong, 2021, cited by the authors) combined with cutoff augmentation (Shen et al., 2020), applied to VLA conditioning embeddings. The individual ingredients are established; the contribution is primarily their composition and empirical validation, which may fall short of the originality bar for the main track.

Several gains are small and potentially within noise. On LIBERO the improvement is 94.3→94.7 avg with mixed per-suite results (Spatial and Object drop), and on real-robot generalization tasks some conditions show near-parity or partial-only improvements (e.g., Language full success 41.6 vs 37.5). Error bars are not reported for the LIBERO or from-scratch comparisons, making it hard to judge statistical significance in these settings.

The results are heavily tied to a single strong baseline (GR00T N1.5). While π₀-FAST results (Table 10) and backbone sweeps help, the largest claims ('state-of-the-art', +4.0 avg on RoboCasa) rest on one training framework, and comparisons to prior reported numbers (e.g., π₀-FAST, FLARE, DUST) are not always like-for-like in data or training budget.

The soft-weight design introduces an unexplored inductive bias: pairs are weighted purely by current-state distance (Table 4a), yet the paper argues multi-modal future actions make next-action targets unreliable. The interaction between this bias and task structure (e.g., symmetric tasks where distant states require similar actions) is not analyzed.

Ablation 'No token aug' (66.3) is close to vanilla InfoNCE (66.7) in Table 4a, suggesting the distance-soft-weighting scheme—the paper's headline novelty—contributes less than the overall contrastive framework; this somewhat undercuts the framing that RS-CL's key distinction is the proprioceptive weighting.

Figures 4, 6, and 7 report means with limited trial/seed transparency in the main text; the detailed seed study is confined to a single low-data setting (Table 8), so the robustness of the headline +13.3% real-robot gain is difficult to fully verify.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: RS-CL uses relative proprioceptive distances as soft supervision weights in a contrastive objective, which is a principled and lightweight way to steer VLM representations toward control-relevant signals without extra forward passes through the backbone.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: state-of-the-art results on RoboCasa-Kitchen (48.2/63.9/65.7 -> 53.0/67.2/69.7 across data regimes), consistent gains on LIBERO, real-robot experiments on a Franka platform with both in-domain and generalization tasks, and from-scratch experiments across multiple VLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B, SigLIP2, GR00T N1.5) demonstrating generality.

Strong analyses supporting the central hypothesis: the visualization of pre-trained VLM embeddings clustering by visual appearance rather than task progress (Fig. 2, Fig. 14), KNN task-phase classification, and CKNNA alignment measurements provide convincing mechanistic evidence that RS-CL actually reshapes representations as claimed, not just aggregate success-rate improvements.

Efficiency is well characterized: Table 6 shows only +1.25% wall-clock overhead, and the TCN comparison (Table 3) demonstrates better success rates at a fraction of the FLOPs of alternative contrastive approaches.

Thorough ablations: soft-label target choices, augmentation strategies, hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 8), seed robustness, multiple action-modeling paradigms (flow matching and autoregressive pi0-FAST, Table 10), and higher-dimensional state configurations (DexMimicGen, Table 11).

Good reproducibility: training details, hyperparameters, dataset sources, evaluation protocol (1200 trials RoboCasa, 50 trials/task LIBERO, 24 trials/real task), and public checkpoints are documented; limitations are honestly discussed in Appendix E.6.
The lambda cosine-decay schedule and the from-scratch vs fine-tuning split show the method works in multiple training scenarios, strengthening the practical relevance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest: the method is essentially a soft-weighted supervised contrastive loss (extending Khosla et al. / Oord et al.) plus a cutoff-style augmentation applied at the feature level. The individual components are well-known; the contribution lies in their combination and application to VLAs rather than a new learning principle.

Some gains could partly stem from giving the model additional implicit access to proprioceptive structure during training rather than genuinely better 'representations'; while the KNN/CKNNA analyses mitigate this concern, a more direct causal disentanglement (e.g., performance when the RS-CL projection branch is removed at test time vs. kept) would strengthen the claim.

From-scratch improvements in Fig. 7 start from very low baselines (e.g., 6.6 -> 11.8, 2.0 -> 2.6), so absolute performance remains weak in those settings; the claims there rest mostly on relative improvements.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art' on RoboCasa-Kitchen relies partly on the authors' own reproductions of baselines (pi0, pi0-FAST) under their training recipe, which introduces potential reproduction discrepancies; the appendix does document these, but independent numbers would be stronger.

The method assumes multi-view observations for view-cutoff augmentation; applicability to single-camera setups (common in many real deployments) is not directly evaluated, and the real-robot gain in the language-following generalization condition is within noise (39.6 vs 37.5 partial).
No explicit statement about code release, which would aid reproducibility given the number of implementation details that affect results.
